title: Did I miss any examples? #broadway #musicaltheatre #theatre
transcript: There's a really rare, very specific type of jukebox musical that I find most fascinating, and I can only think of 4 examples of it in existence. And that is where they use pre existing music, but they write original lyrics just for the show. And what I find fascinating is that in theory, this would massively alleviate one of the biggest obstacles with jukebox musicals, which is trying to make the songs make sense in this new narrative context. And you think: all you gotta do is change the lyrics to fit the context. Easy peasy! But I've seen several dozen jukebox musicals, and only four of them I can think of really leaned into this approach in a major way. We have the 2019 version of Clueless the musical starring Dove Cameron. Not to be confused with the current London version of Clueless the musical, which has an original score. This earlier version actually played in New York, off/Broadway, and it used songs from the 90s but wrote new lyrics for them. I don't really think it worked, though, because it was mostly played for laughs, and yet it was just not that funny. It was actually pretty cringey. A somewhat better usage of this device came a few years later with once upon a one more time, which changed the lyrics to some of these Britney Spears hits to fit the fairy tale narrative. It was definitely pretty corny and silly here too, but I think the humor landed somewhat better, and it successfully made the songs make more sense in the narrative. But both of those examples were comedic. What about more serious musicals? I can only think of two more serious examples. We had Jelly's last jam, about Jelly Roll Morton, and here's a deep cut for you. Soul Doctor, about the singing Rabbi Shlomo Carlebach, Which incidentally featured Amber Iman in a breakout performance as Nina Simone. And in both of these cases, they liberally incorporated purpose-written lyrics and otherwise adapted the songs to fit story. And in my opinion, both shows did it successfully. Soul Doctor may not have been highly regarded in general, but in my opinion at least, the musicalization of this story with the Shlomo Carlebach melodies was not one of its problems. Even so, looking back at these four examples altogether, maybe it's not so surprising that shows rarely use this approach when, whether it's correlation or causation, the shows that have used it have not been very well-received. And the one that was better received, Jelly's last jam, is the most unconventional. It predates the main influx of jukebox musicals by a number of years, and it's a more serious and even critical examination of Jelly Roll Morton. Not exactly trying to appease a fan base, Soul Doctor likewise had more flexibility in the sense that I think they were trying to expose more people to the story of Shlomo Carlebach more so than they were trying to financially capitalize on an existing fanbase. But of course that was also a disadvantage to them commercially. And then the other two examples being more comedic also theoretically gives them room to play around, although neither of them were that successful anyway. And while I didn't mind the new lyrics for the Britney songs, I imagine that while it was designed to make for more seamless storytelling for some Britney fans, it probably had the opposite effect of taking them out of the show.
